edges.description: Presentation of gluten peptides on the permissive haplotype licenses the gluten-sensitive autoimmune response.
The gut autoimmune response produces celiac-type villous atrophy in most DH patients.
The gut autoimmune response evolves into a high-avidity IgA response against epidermal transglutaminase.
The chronic gluten-driven enteropathy carries a six- to tenfold increased risk of enteropathy-associated lymphoma, concentrated in the years before a gluten-free diet is established.
High-avidity IgA anti-TG3 complexes with the TG3 enzyme and deposits in the papillary dermis.

nodes.description: In DH the IgA response acquires markedly higher avidity for epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) than for tissue transglutaminase, and a TG3-specific antibody population appears. This is the molecular feature that distinguishes DH from celiac disease without skin involvement.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermal transglutaminase (TGase 3) is the autoantigen of dermatitis herpetiformis.
evidence.snippet: antibodies in patients having dermatitis herpetiformis show a markedly higher avidity for epidermal transglutaminase

nodes.description: Dapsone rapidly controls the rash and itch at onset by suppressing neutrophil function; most patients can stop it after about two years once a strict gluten-free diet controls the disease.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: At onset, most patients need additional dapsone to rapidly control the rash and itching

nodes.description: Dietary gluten is the necessary environmental trigger. It drives the small-bowel autoimmunity that underlies DH, and its removal (a gluten-free diet) heals both the rash and the enteropathy.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermal transglutaminase (TGase 3) is the autoantigen of dermatitis herpetiformis.
evidence.snippet: evoked and maintained by gluten

nodes.description: DH arises from latent or manifest celiac disease in the gut: gluten exposure drives an IgA autoantibody response against tissue transglutaminase, with small-bowel villous atrophy or celiac-type inflammation in most patients.

evidence.snippet: DH and CD share a similar genetic background, small bowel mucosal alterations, and an autoimmune response against tissue transglutaminase in the serum and small bowel

nodes.description: A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the treatment of choice for all DH patients. It heals both the rash and the small-bowel enteropathy and lowers lymphoma risk, though its effect on the rash is slow.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: the treatment of choice for all patients is a gluten-free diet

nodes.description: IgA anti-TG3 and the TG3 enzyme form tightly bound immune complexes that precipitate as pathognomonic granular IgA deposits in the papillary dermis. Passive transfer of anti-TG3 reproduces these deposits, establishing them as directly antibody-driven.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis herpetiformis sera or goat anti-transglutaminase-3 transferred to human skin-grafted mice mimics dermatitis herpetiformis immunopathology.
evidence.snippet: All mice that received goat anti-TG3 produced papillary dermal immune deposits, and these deposits reacted with both rabbit anti-TG3 and DH patient sera.

nodes.description: Dietary iodide and certain NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin) are recognized exacerbating triggers that worsen the rash and itch in established DH.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: Triggering factors such as taking indomethacin and inadvertent dietary iodide ingestion are known to exacerbate the rash and itching

nodes.description: Like celiac disease, DH carries a six- to tenfold increased risk of lymphoma (enteropathy-associated T-cell and B-cell types / non-Hodgkin lymphoma). The excess risk is concentrated in the first years after diagnosis and is reduced by strict gluten-free-diet adherence; overall DH mortality is not elevated.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: The risk in DH is increased six to tenfold.
Mortality due to non-Hodgkin lymphomas was increased only during the first 5 years following the diagnosis but not thereafter

nodes.description: The dermal immune deposits drive a predominant neutrophilic infiltrate into the dermal papillae, forming the papillary microabscesses characteristic of DH histopathology. Gut-derived IL-8 primes neutrophils, which bind the deposited IgA directly through their Fc-alpha receptor (CD89, FCAR).
nodes.id: Neutrophil Recruitment and Papillary Microabscess Formation

evidence.snippet: a predominant neutrophilic infiltrate at the dermal papillae at histopathology
Circulating and skin resident neutrophils express Fc IgA receptor (CD89), suggesting a direct interaction between neutrophils and IgA.
Activation of innate immunity in the gut leads to increased release of IL-8, which is thought to be responsible for the initial priming of neutrophils

nodes.description: Symmetrical grouped papules and vesicles on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks, sacral region); the clinical hallmark of DH.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, DH presents with polymorphic lesions, including papules, vesicles, and small blisters, symmetrically distributed in typical anatomical sites including the extensor aspects of the limbs, the elbows, the sacral regions, and the buttocks.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: The mean age at onset is about 50 years.

nodes.description: Intense itch, often so severe that scratching destroys the primary lesions and leaves excoriations.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis herpetiformis. Part I. Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and clinical presentation.
evidence.snippet: young adults present with excoriations only, as the severe pruritus effectively destroys any primary lesions

nodes.description: An anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody reported in a single refractory case of DH resistant to gluten-free diet, dapsone, sulfasalazine, and conventional immunosuppressants. It depletes CD20+ B cells (the autoantibody-producing lineage), not the terminally differentiated plasma cells.

evidence.snippet: rituximab has been proven to be effective in a patient resistant to GFD, dapsone, sulfasalazine, and conventional immunosuppressive agents such as azathioprine

nodes.description: Most DH patients have celiac-type small-bowel changes, ranging from villous atrophy to increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, usually without overt gastrointestinal symptoms.

evidence.reference_title: Dermatitis Herpetiformis: An Update on Diagnosis and Management.
evidence.snippet: three-fourths of patients with DH have villous atrophy in the small bowel, and the rest have celiac-type inflammatory changes

nodes.description: Neutrophil-mediated damage at the dermal papillae produces subepidermal vesicles that present clinically as grouped papules and small blisters, though intense scratching often destroys the primary lesions.

evidence.snippet: Activated neutrophils release neutrophil elastase and granzyme B, which induce subepidermal split by cleaving adhesion molecules of the BMZ, such as collagen VII

nodes.description: A sulfonamide used as a dapsone alternative when dapsone is not tolerated or is contraindicated; it carries a lower monitoring burden than dapsone but can still cause hemolytic anemia and gastrointestinal upset.

evidence.snippet: Possible alternatives to dapsone are the so-called sulfonamides, including sulfasalazine, sulfapyridine, and sulfamethoxypyridazine
